title: Things That Help: Lisa Van Gemert's Content Capsules Method or-creating-joyful-knowledge-rich-learning-spaces-remotely-or-in-persoon
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: This post shares an excerpt, the third chapter, of gifted-education specialist Lisa Van Gemert's book on the 'Concept Capsule' method for teaching academic vocabulary, introduced by Dave Stuart Jr. as aligned with his own knowledge-rich curriculum philosophy. Van Gemert lays out a six-step cycle, introduce, review, quiz, include, use, test, for cycling a fixed bank of roughly 80 Tier III vocabulary terms through a school year, grounding the review cadence explicitly in Hermann Ebbinghaus's forgetting-curve research: review must start immediately after initial instruction, after which spacing can gradually widen. She addresses the practical objection teachers raise first, time, by showing how most of the method piggybacks on instructional moments already built into a class period, quizzes, dead time, bell ringers, rather than requiring new blocks of instructional time. Grading design gets specific treatment too: she recommends aggregating small quiz scores across a grading period rather than counting each quiz individually, keeping stakes low enough that students experience the frequent quizzing as a confidence-builder. The excerpt closes by tying method to mindset, arguing that a teacher's enthusiasm when introducing a new term functions as part of the technique itself, since students 'read us like they do the weather.'
points: Van Gemert's Concept Capsule method, excerpted from her book and shared via Stuart's blog, is built on a six-step cycle, introduce, review, quiz, include, use, test, designed to keep a fixed set of Tier III academic vocabulary terms 'in play' all year rather than taught once and dropped.

The method is explicitly grounded in Ebbinghaus's forgetting-curve research: review must begin immediately after initial instruction and can then space out over time, which Van Gemert contrasts with the common teach-then-test-months-later default.

Time cost is addressed directly and practically; introduction takes about ten minutes per term, review activities run under twenty minutes, and much of the retrieval practice piggybacks on quizzes and tests teachers are already giving.

Grading design matters to student buy-in: Van Gemert recommends aggregating quiz scores across a grading period rather than counting each short quiz individually, keeping the stakes low enough that students experience the quizzes as confidence-builders rather than gotchas.

The excerpt frames teacher attitude as a delivery mechanism for the method's effectiveness; students 'read us like they do the weather,' so introducing terms with genuine curiosity and enthusiasm is treated as functionally part of the technique, not just good vibes.
quotes: In a nutshell, you choose critical vocabulary, explicitly teach it, review it often in ways students enjoy, use it regularly, and quiz it frequently.
The review activities do not need to be time consuming, but they need to be frequent. It's far better to have frequent, short review experiences than a single, extended experience.
In the 1880's, Herman Ebbinghaus conducted a series of experiments (on himself!) to test how quickly people forget learned information. He found that the rate of forgetting was shocking.

Ebbinghaus believed that every review experience meant you could space further review farther apart (so you need to review less and less frequently as you move on). You do, however, need to review close to initial instruction.
What most teachers do is teach something, assign a practice assignment, perhaps review that assignment, and then move on until there is a test. Then, they give a review of all of that learning.
With Concept Capsules, we review frequently, and we begin the review immediately.

To the brain, there is no such thing as "easy" or "hard." There is only "familiar" and "unfamiliar." By using the Concept Capsule method, I ensure to the greatest extent possible that my students enjoy a sense of ease so their abilities can shine through.

They must be introduced from a place of encouragement and even excitement. If your attitude is, "Well, here's one more thing they're expecting me to do," your students will feed off that attitude. It's contagious.
